label: nested in command substitution
why: The example guard tokenizes only the TOP-LEVEL command. Here the downloader lives inside $(...), so it never appears as a top-level token and the shell that runs is `sh -c` (which reads its script from an argument, not a pipe). A real guard closes this with a quote-aware parser that recurses into every executable context.

label: nested in backticks
why: Same class, backtick spelling: the fetch is inside a command substitution and `bash -c` takes its script as an argument, so the top-level token scan sees neither a piped downloader nor a stdin-reading shell.

label: two-step via variable
why: Fetch and execution are two separate statements joined by a variable, with no pipe between them. Catching this needs cross-statement taint tracking, which trades false positives for coverage — a deliberate design call, not an oversight.
